tips.title: The Anthology is not the original key
tips.body: *Defying Gravity* was written in **D flat major** and **transposed to D major** for the Anthology. A question can ask for either, so know both and know which is which.

tips.title: Three verses, four choruses
tips.body: Verses at bars **34, 63 and 135**; choruses at **50, 79, 103 and 151**. They do **not** alternate evenly, and assuming they do is the commonest structural error here.

tips.title: The metre moves three times
tips.body: **3/2**, then **2/2**, then **4/4** at bar 88, then back to **2/2** at bar 115. Never write that the song is in one time signature throughout.

tips.title: B minor, but a D major chord
tips.body: The Maestoso finale from bar 168 is in **B minor** — and the very last chord is **D major**, the relative major. The song turns to the major at the final moment.

tips.title: Tie every effect to the drama
tips.body: Ambiguous tonality while Elphaba is undecided; the tonic at bar 32 as she finds her position; huge rising leaps as she sings of rising; the full band at bar 135 where she decides. Naming the effect earns a mark, linking it to the story earns the band.

steps.title: Where this sits, and what is happening on stage
steps.body:
This is a set work for **Area of Study 3: Music for Stage and Screen**, alongside John Williams's *Star Wars* main title. **Music theatre** integrates songs, spoken dialogue, acting and dance within a popular idiom; a **musical** is an extended piece of music theatre.

**Stephen Schwartz** is an American music theatre composer and lyricist. Born in New York in **1948**, he studied piano and composition at the Juilliard School while still at high school, then graduated in drama from Carnegie Mellon. His first success was *Godspell* in **1972**. In the 1990s he worked with Alan Menken, and returned to that collaboration in 2007 for the lyrics of *Enchanted*. In **2003** he was **both composer and lyricist** for *Wicked*, and won a Grammy for his work as composer, lyricist and producer.

**Wicked** is based on the novel *Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West*. It retells *The Wizard of Oz* from the point of view of the two witches — **Elphaba**, who becomes the Wicked Witch of the West, and **Glinda**, the Good Witch.

**Defying Gravity is the finale of Act 1.** Elphaba has just discovered that the Wizard of Oz is not the heroic figure she believed him to be. She vows to fight him and his plans, and sings of wanting to live without limits, against the rules other people have set for her. Knowing the dramatic situation matters: almost every musical decision in the song serves it.

**One fact that is asked about directly.** It was originally written in **D flat major**, but it has been **transposed to D major** in the Anthology. So the key you study is not the key it was written in.

steps.title: The voices, and the orchestra
steps.body:
**It is a duet** for Elphaba and Glinda, **with some spoken dialogue as well as singing**. The two characters deliver their text in **three ways**:

- **spoken**
- **half sung and half spoken**, notated on the stave with **crosses instead of note heads**
- **entirely sung**

That notation detail is worth knowing: a cross-headed note means pitch is approximate. The singers need **extremely versatile voices**, with a range of just under **two octaves**, from the G below middle C to the F above.

**Wicked uses a large orchestra**, and the guide is specific:

- **woodwind**, including piccolo, bass clarinet and cor anglais
- **brass** and **strings**
- **harp** and **three keyboards**
- **percussion**: drum kit, tubular bells and timpani
- **electric guitars**, which give a modern sound and here need **overdrive**, a distortion effect

**The score in the Anthology is a short score**, also called an **orchestral reduction** — the full orchestral parts compressed onto fewer staves, with the main solo instruments labelled.

**The orchestra is used for drama, and each effect has a place:**

- **brass** play homophonic chordal music, almost **fanfare-like**, at bar 20
- **strings** use **tremolo** to add tension at bar 34
- the **closed hi-hat** plays constant crotchets at bar 51 to drive the music forward
- a **cymbal roll** adds excitement into a key change at bar 122
- the **full band** plays at the climax at bar 135
- **synthesisers and glockenspiel** give the chorus a high, magical-sounding repeated quaver accompaniment
- **tubular bells** give an ethereal sonority at bar 147

steps.title: Structure: verse and chorus, inside eight tempo changes
steps.body:
**The form is verse and chorus**, and the first thing to notice is that there are **more choruses than verses**: **three verses** (bars 34, 63 and 135) against **four choruses** (bars 50, 79, 103 and 151).

But the verse-chorus scheme sits inside a larger design built from **tempo changes**, and those tempo changes are what actually shape the song. There are **nine tempo markings**, and the guide says they are *important to the overall structure*.


**Notice the pattern**: the music keeps alternating between slower, free, recitative-like writing and fast, driving sections. Each time it returns to **Andante** it is bringing back the homophonic chordal music from bar 20, and each **Allegro** takes it forward again. The song gets its momentum from that alternation, not from one continuous build.

**Rallentandos** are used, particularly at the ends of sections, to move from **Allegro** back to **Andante**, sometimes followed by *a tempo*. There is a rallentando at the end of the piece too.

steps.title: Section by section
steps.body:
Each section is defined by its **tempo**, its **mood** and its **melodic material**.

- **Bars 1 to 19 — free tempo (*colla voce*), recitative-like.** A duet between Glinda and Elphaba mixing spoken dialogue and singing. Orchestral **chord stabs** at the start with sparse monophonic moments; the accompaniment then becomes chordal and sustained.
- **Bars 20 to 48 — Andante. Verse at bar 34.** A homophonic chordal opening that moves through different major keys. The melody is **legato and conjunct**. The verse has **tremolo strings with dissonant harmony**.
- **Bars 49 to 87 — Allegro. Chorus at 50, verse at 63, chorus at 79.** The title **hook** — a leaping melody — is sung over a **broken chord** accompaniment with driving hi-hat. Glinda then sings a **crotchet triplet** melody before Elphaba takes over with a **syncopated** version of the verse, leading into the chorus.
- **Bars 88 to 102 — Moderato.** A contrasting section in the **new key of G major**, both characters singing a new melody **in unison** over a **semiquaver** accompaniment.
- **Bars 103 to 110 — Allegro. Chorus at 103.** Back to **D major**, both characters, opening in unison with strong piano accompaniment.
- **Bars 111 to 128 — Andante.** The homophonic chordal music from earlier returns, leading into the recitative-like music of the opening.
- **Bars 129 to 161 — Allegro. Verse at 135, chorus at 151.** The **climax**, with full orchestra and loud dynamic. It opens with the homophonic chordal music, then an **extended version of the verse in a higher register** with developed melodic and rhythmic ideas, then a reprise of the chorus.
- **Bars 162 to 177 — Andante to Maestoso.** A build to a **full tutti finale**, in **B minor at bar 168**, with Elphaba, Glinda, the ensemble chorus and orchestra **in counterpoint**, each with different musical lines and different lyrics.

**The shape to remember**: free and spoken, then lyrical, then driving, then a contrasting key, then a return, then the climax, then a contrapuntal finale.

steps.title: Tonality: ambiguous, then restless, then home
steps.body:
**The song is in D major**, but it takes a while to get there and it does not stay put.

**At the start the tonality is ambiguous**, with **chromatic movement** and **unrelated chord progressions**. That is a deliberate dramatic effect: Elphaba has not decided anything yet.

Then it moves, and the guide is precise about where:

- **bar 20** — B major, for two bars
- **bar 22** — F major
- **bar 32** — arrives in the **tonic, D major**, for the verse
- stays in **D major until bar 88**, when it moves to **G major**
- **bar 103** — returns to **D major**
- **bar 115** — the chromatic melody of the opening returns
- **bar 132** — back to the **tonic, D major**
- **bar 168** — **B minor** for the Maestoso finale, finishing on a chord of **D major**

**Two things are worth noticing.** First, the song **ends on a D major chord even though the final section is in B minor** — B minor is the relative minor of D major, so the ending turns to the major at the last moment. Second, the **chromatic opening material comes back at bar 115**, which links the end of the song to its beginning.

**Harmony.** The chords are **in root position**. Progressions are often **unrelated**, and at the opening there are shifts **downwards in parallel semitones** — for example a **D chord to a C sharp minor chord to a C major chord**. There is some **dissonance**, at bar 30. At the end there is a **pedal** at bar 168.

steps.title: Melody, rhythm and metre
steps.body:
**Melody.**

- The text setting is **syllabic throughout**, with rhythms moving in a **speech-like** manner.
- There is **vocalisation** at the end, at bar 175, on the word *aah*.
- The melody starts **conjunct**, moving by step.
- Bars 6 and 7 show an **ascending sequence**.
- The verse and chorus **combine conjunct movement with wide, angular leaps**.
- Leaps often feature a **rising perfect fifth**, as at bar 34. Some are exceptionally large: a **compound perfect fourth** at bars 39 to 40, and a **compound perfect fifth** at bars 140 to 141.

A **compound** interval is one larger than an octave — so a compound perfect fifth is an octave plus a fifth. Those enormous leaps are the song's most recognisable feature, and they suit the words: Elphaba is singing about rising.

**Metre.** The time signature **changes**, and this is often asked about:

- the opening section moves from **3/2 triple time** to **2/2 duple time**
- it stays in **2/2 until bar 88**, where it changes to **4/4 quadruple time**
- at **bar 115** it returns to **2/2 duple time**

**Rhythm.**

- **Syncopation** is frequent throughout, for example at bars 67 to 70.
- **Dotted rhythms** are used throughout — for example at bar 82, on the word *gra-vi-ty*.
- **Triplets** appear as both **quaver triplets**, at bar 96, and **crotchet triplets**, at bar 60.
- Rhythms are mostly **crotchet and quaver** based, with longer notes at the ends of phrases.
- **Rests** often break up the phrases.
- **Each phrase starts off the beat**, after a crotchet rest — for example at bar 15.
- **Pause marks**, or fermatas, lengthen and free the longer rhythms at the end, at bars 174 and 176.

steps.title: Texture
steps.body:
The textures change with the sections, and each has a clear place.

- **Sparse**, at the opening, with punctuating instrumental **chord stabs** at bar 1, and some **monophonic unaccompanied** bars at bar 3.
- **Melody and accompaniment**, also called **melody-dominated homophony**, in the verses: the singer accompanied by chords in the orchestra.
- **Homophonic chordal** moments, where everything moves together, at bar 132.
- **Ostinato** accompaniment at bar 88, with repeated **semiquavers**.
- **Unison**, where Elphaba and Glinda sing the same notes, at bar 101, and **harmony in thirds** at bar 127. Mostly, though, the two sing **separately**.
- **Contrapuntal** at the end: **three different musical ideas with different lyrics** at bar 168.

**The ending is the one to know.** At bar 168 Elphaba, Glinda, the ensemble chorus and the orchestra all sing and play **different lines with different words at the same time**. That is genuine counterpoint, it is the fullest texture in the song, and it is a standard device for a musical's Act 1 finale: several characters, each with their own view of what has just happened, heard together.

steps.title: Your turn: the song from memory
steps.body:
**Part A.** Write out the nine tempo markings in order, with their bar numbers.

**Part B.** One sentence each:

1. Who wrote the music, and who wrote the words?
2. What key is the song in, and what key was it originally written in?
3. Where does the song come in the musical, and what has just happened to Elphaba?
4. Name the three ways the characters deliver their text.

**Part C.** Harder:

5. The song is in verse and chorus form. How many of each, and at which bars?
6. Describe how the metre changes through the song.
7. What is unusual about the key of the last section and the final chord?

**Part D.** Write a paragraph explaining how Schwartz uses the orchestra dramatically, naming at least four effects and giving a bar for each.

For question 2, remember the Anthology is not in the original key.

steps.title: Going deeper: music serving the drama
steps.body:
**Every musical choice here serves the story**, and saying so is what lifts an answer. Elphaba has just learned the Wizard is a fraud and decides to defy him.

- **The opening is tonally ambiguous** — chromatic, with unrelated progressions. Elphaba has not decided yet. The music is unsettled because she is.
- **The tonic, D major, arrives at bar 32**, for the verse. She has begun to find her position.
- **The huge leaps** — a compound perfect fourth at bars 39 to 40, a compound perfect fifth at bars 140 to 141 — are literal word-painting. She sings of rising, and the melody rises further than a melody normally can.
- **The driving hi-hat crotchets at bar 51** give the chorus forward momentum, which is the moment she commits.
- **The chromatic opening material returns at bar 115**, dragging the doubt back just before the climax.
- **The full band at bar 135** is the decision made.
- **Counterpoint at bar 168**: three sets of words at once, because three parties now want different things.

**Two facts that are pure marks.** The original key is **D flat major** and the Anthology is in **D major**. And there are **four choruses but only three verses** — students assume they alternate evenly.

**Do not say it is in one time signature.** The metre moves 3/2, then 2/2, then 4/4 at bar 88, then back to 2/2 at bar 115.

**The crosses instead of note heads** are worth a sentence. They mark writing that is **half sung and half spoken**, which is a music theatre convention for heightened speech — more intense than dialogue, less formal than song. It belongs to the genre, and naming it shows you know what music theatre is, rather than just this song.

**The score is a short score, an orchestral reduction.** So a question about instrumentation is testing whether you know what the labels mean, not whether you can read a full orchestral layout.

**For Section B**, the comparison question, this piece sits in the same area of study as *Star Wars*. Both use a large orchestra dramatically, but for different ends: Williams characterises with **leitmotif** in music without words, while Schwartz has **words, voices and a stage**, so his orchestra reacts to a text. Comparing what each composer can and cannot do is a stronger line than listing instruments.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Area of Study 3: Music for Stage and Screen.** The other set work is *Star Wars*.
- **Stephen Schwartz** wrote **both music and lyrics**; *Wicked*, **2003**.
- It is the **finale of Act 1**, after Elphaba learns the Wizard is a fraud.
- A **duet** for Elphaba and Glinda, with **spoken dialogue** as well as singing.
- Text is delivered **spoken**, **half sung and half spoken** (crosses for note heads), or **entirely sung**.
- Vocal range: just under **two octaves**, G below middle C to the F above.
- Originally **D flat major**; the Anthology transposes it to **D major**.
- **Verse and chorus** form: verses at **34, 63, 135**; choruses at **50, 79, 103, 151**.
- **Nine tempo markings**, from **Free tempo** to **Maestoso**, and they shape the song.
- Large orchestra: woodwind with piccolo, bass clarinet and cor anglais; brass; strings; harp; **three keyboards**; drum kit, tubular bells, timpani; **electric guitars with overdrive**.
- The Anthology score is a **short score**, an **orchestral reduction**.
- Tonality is **ambiguous** at the start; the tonic arrives at **bar 32**; **G major** at 88; back to **D** at 103; **B minor** at 168, ending on a **D major** chord.
- Chords are in **root position**; progressions often **unrelated**; parallel semitone shifts at the opening; a **pedal** at bar 168.
- Text setting is **syllabic**; **vocalisation** on *aah* at bar 175.
- Leaps include a **rising perfect fifth** (34), a **compound perfect fourth** (39 to 40) and a **compound perfect fifth** (140 to 141).
- Metre: **3/2**, then **2/2**, then **4/4** at bar 88, then **2/2** at bar 115.
- **Syncopation**, **dotted rhythms**, **quaver and crotchet triplets**; each phrase starts **off the beat**.
- Textures: **sparse chord stabs**, **monophonic**, **melody-dominated homophony**, **ostinato** at 88, **unison** at 101, **thirds** at 127, and **contrapuntal** at **168**.

questions.prompt: Explain how Stephen Schwartz uses the orchestra to serve the drama in Defying Gravity. Name at least four effects and say where each occurs.
questions.solution: Wicked uses a large orchestra, and Schwartz draws on it selectively so that each effect marks a moment in the story. At bar 20 the brass play homophonic chordal music in an almost fanfare-like manner, which lends weight and formality just as the song begins to take shape after the free opening. At bar 34, under the first verse, the strings play tremolo with dissonant harmony, creating tension at the point where Elphaba is still uncertain. At bar 51 the closed hi-hat of the drum kit plays constant crotchets, adding rhythmic momentum and driving the first chorus forward as she begins to commit to her decision. At bar 122 a cymbal roll adds excitement as the music moves into a key change. The full band plays at bar 135, the climax of the song, where Elphaba's decision is made and the dynamic is loud. At bar 147 tubular bells give an ethereal sonority. Throughout the choruses, synthesisers and glockenspiel provide a high, magical-sounding repeated quaver accompaniment which suits a story about witches, while electric guitars with overdrive, a distortion effect, give the whole song a modern rock-influenced sound rather than a traditional music theatre one. The orchestration therefore tracks Elphaba's emotional journey from uncertainty to resolve.

- **bar 20** — **brass**, homophonic chordal, almost **fanfare-like**: weight and formality as the song takes shape.

- through the choruses — **synthesisers and glockenspiel**, high repeated quavers, magical-sounding.
- throughout — **electric guitars with overdrive**, a distortion effect giving a modern sound.

**What earns the top band** is linking the effects to the story rather than listing them: the orchestration tracks Elphaba's journey from uncertainty to resolve, and the loudest, fullest scoring arrives exactly where her decision does.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of Defying Gravity, explaining how the tempo changes shape the song.
questions.solution: The song is in verse and chorus form, with three verses at bars 34, 63 and 135 and four choruses at bars 50, 79, 103 and 151, so the two do not alternate evenly. Within that scheme the song is shaped by nine tempo markings, which define sections contrasting in tempo, mood and melodic material. It begins at bar 1 in a free tempo, colla voce and recitative-like, with spoken dialogue and singing over orchestral chord stabs. At bar 20 an Andante brings homophonic chordal writing and the first verse, with tremolo strings. At bar 49 an Allegro brings the first chorus, whose leaping title hook is sung over broken chords and a driving hi-hat. At bar 88 a Moderato provides contrast in the new key of G major, with both characters in unison over semiquavers. At bar 103 the Allegro and the chorus return in D major. At bar 111 an Andante brings back the chordal music and then the recitative-like opening material. At bar 129 the Allegro returns for the climax, with full orchestra, an extended verse in a higher register and a reprise of the chorus. Finally, from bar 162 an Andante builds to a Maestoso at bar 168 for a contrapuntal tutti finale. The alternation between slower, freer, chordal writing and faster, driving sections is what gives the song its momentum: it does not build continuously but repeatedly gathers pace, falls back and gathers again, which mirrors Elphaba's wavering before she commits.

questions.prompt: Both Defying Gravity and the Star Wars main title are set works for Music for Stage and Screen, and both use a large orchestra. Compare how the two composers use their orchestras, and explain why their aims differ.
questions.solution: Both set works use a large orchestra dramatically, but they are doing different jobs, because one has words and a stage and the other does not. In the Star Wars main title Williams has no text and no singers, so the orchestra must do all the characterising itself. He relies on leitmotif, on a bold brass-led fanfare and on orchestral colour to establish a world and a mood before any story has been told. The listener is being oriented by the music alone. Schwartz, by contrast, is writing for two characters who sing, speak and act, so his orchestra reacts to a text that is already carrying the meaning. His effects are therefore local and precisely placed: fanfare-like brass at bar 20, tremolo strings with dissonant harmony under the uncertain first verse at bar 34, a driving closed hi-hat at bar 51 as Elphaba commits, a cymbal roll into a key change at bar 122, the full band at the climax at bar 135, and tubular bells for an ethereal sonority at bar 147. Schwartz also uses forces Williams does not, including three keyboards, synthesisers, glockenspiel and electric guitars with overdrive, which give Wicked a modern, popular sound appropriate to music theatre rather than to a symphonic film score. A further difference is that Schwartz must leave room for the voices, so his textures are often melody-dominated homophony, whereas Williams can fill the whole texture. Both, however, reserve their fullest scoring for the dramatic peak.

**Williams has no words and no singers.** The orchestra must characterise on its own, so he uses **leitmotif** and a bold **brass-led** sound to establish a world before any story is told. The listener is oriented by music alone.

**Schwartz has words, voices and a stage.** The meaning is already carried by the text, so his orchestral effects are **local and precisely placed**:

- fanfare-like **brass** at bar 20
- **tremolo strings** with dissonance under the uncertain verse at bar 34

- a **cymbal roll** into the key change at bar 122
- the **full band** at the climax at bar 135
- **tubular bells** at bar 147

**Two further differences worth making:**

- Schwartz uses **three keyboards, synthesisers, glockenspiel and electric guitars with overdrive** — a modern, popular sound belonging to music theatre rather than to a symphonic film score.

examTechnique.body:
Give Stephen Schwartz as both composer and lyricist.

Say the song was written in D flat major and transposed to D major in the Anthology.

Count the verses and choruses separately: three verses and four choruses.

Track the metre changes rather than naming one time signature.

Use bar numbers for every effect you name, since the guide gives them and the marks follow them.

Link each orchestral effect to what is happening to Elphaba at that point.

For the finale, say it is in B minor but ends on a D major chord.

Describe the ending as contrapuntal, with three different ideas and three different sets of lyrics.
examinerErrors: Saying the song is in D flat major, which is the original key but not the Anthology's.
Assuming the verses and choruses alternate evenly.
Writing that the song is in 4/4 throughout.
Saying the song ends in B minor, when the final chord is D major.
Describing the Anthology score as a full orchestral score rather than a short score.
Listing orchestral effects without saying where they occur or what they do.
Missing that the chromatic opening material returns at bar 115.
Calling the finale homophonic rather than contrapuntal.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the song as drama set to music. It knows the opening is tonally ambiguous because Elphaba has not decided, that the tonic arrives once she has, and that the huge compound leaps are word-painting for a character singing about rising. It counts three verses against four choruses rather than assuming symmetry, tracks the metre through its three changes, and knows the Anthology is a semitone above the original. It gives a bar number for every effect it names, and it recognises the contrapuntal finale for what it is: a standard Act 1 device in which several characters, each wanting something different, are heard at once.
